newsitem.title: DENMARK: Britain's Rushdie in Denmark to get literary award.
newsitem.headline: Britain's Rushdie in Denmark to get literary award.

text.p: British author Salman Rushdie, shrugging off official concern that he might be the target of an Islamic assassination plot on Danish soil, arrived on Wednesday to collect a European Union literary award in Copenhagen.

Speaking at a news conference ahead of the prizegiving ceremony, he said he accepted the government's apologies for its initial attempts to block the visit but remained sceptical that there was a concrete plan to kill him in Copenhagen,
"I am not convinced, and my information from the other side of the water does not lead me to believe in the existence of any specific threat in Copenhagen, today or tomorrow," he said.
Danish officials have indicated that the initial attempt to shelve a ceremony planned for Thursday was based on warnings from British intelligence.
"I have pushed very hard in Britain and I am satisfied that the British did not inform the Danes of any specific threat," Rushdie said.

Indian-born Rushdie has lived in hiding and under guard since 1989 when Iranian revolutionary leader Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini issued a "fatwa" or death sentence against him for his novel "The Satanic Verses", saying it blasphemed against Islam.

Danish Prime Minister Poul Nyrup Rasmussen, whose minority government came close to falling as a result of its admitted bungling of the affair, was adamant that intelligence reports indicated a specific threat but he was not able to give details.
"The whole question was not only a question of Mr.Rushdie but people around Mr.Rushdie at the ceremony," he said without elaboration.
Taking no chances, the government provided tight security for Rushdie.

Reporters attending morning news conferences with the writer and Rasmussen were first assembled at a government building in the capital where they were searched and scanned with electronic metal detectors and their bags were checked by sniffer-dogs.

Then they were put aboard police buses and driven first to parliament for the meeting with Rasmussen, then to an undisclosed destination which turned out to be a hotel in the distant suburbs of Copenhagen for the Rushdie news conference.
The arts complex on the city's outskirts where the prize ceremony is to be held was chosen because, sited at the end of a spit of land jutting out to sea, it is easy to seal off.

Heavily armed police and security agents have ringed the building since it was announced as the venue on Tuesday, a police helicopter will hover overhead throughout the ceremony and the 500 invited guests and journalists will face rigorous security checks on their way into the auditorium.

Also attending the evening prize ceremony will be Austrian author Christoph Ransmayer and Danish translator Thorkild Bjoernvig, who are sharing the European Union's 20,000 ECU Aristeion literature award with Rushdie.
The ceremony is taking place in Copenhagen as the city is this year's European Cultural Capital.
